{{Short description|Ordered field where every nonnegative element is a square}}{{about|ordered fields|algebraic number fields whose ring of integers has a Euclidean algorithm|Norm-Euclidean field|
the class of models in statistical mechanics|Euclidean field theory}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''Euclidean field''' is an [[ordered field]] {{math|''K''}} for which every non-negative element is a square: that is, {{math|''x'' ≥ 0}} in {{math|''K''}} implies that {{math|1=''x'' = ''y''<sup>2</sup>}} for some {{math|''y''}} in {{math|''K''}}. 

The [[constructible number]]s form a Euclidean field. It is the smallest Euclidean field, as every Euclidean field contains it as an ordered subfield. In other words, the constructible numbers form the [[#Euclidean closure|Euclidean closure]] of the [[rational number]]s.

==Properties==
* Every Euclidean field is an ordered [[Pythagorean field]], but the converse is not true.<ref name=M89>Martin (1998) p.&nbsp;89</ref>
* If ''E''/''F'' is a finite [[field extension|extension]], and ''E'' is Euclidean, then so is ''F''.  This "going-down theorem" is a consequence of the [[Diller–Dress theorem]].<ref name=Lam270>Lam (2005) p.270</ref>

==Examples==
* The real [[constructible numbers]], those (signed) lengths which can be constructed from a rational segment by [[ruler and compass constructions]], form a Euclidean field.<ref name=M3536>Martin (1998) pp.&nbsp;35–36</ref>

Every [[real closed field]] is a Euclidean field. The following examples are also real closed fields.
* The [[real number]]s <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with the usual operations and ordering form a Euclidean field.
* The field of real [[algebraic number]]s <math>\mathbb{R}\cap\mathbb{\overline Q}</math> is a Euclidean field.
* The field of [[hyperreal number]]s is a Euclidean field.

==Counterexamples==
* The [[rational number]]s <math>\mathbb Q</math> with the usual operations and ordering do not form a Euclidean field. For example, 2 is not a square in <math>\mathbb Q</math> since the [[square root of 2]] is [[irrational number|irrational]].<ref name=M35>Martin (1998) p.&nbsp;35</ref>  By the going-down result above, no [[algebraic number field]] can be Euclidean.<ref name=Lam270/>
* The [[complex number]]s <math>\mathbb C</math> do not form a Euclidean field since they cannot be given the structure of an ordered field.

==Euclidean closure==
The '''Euclidean closure''' of an ordered field {{mvar|K}} is an extension of {{mvar|K}} in the [[quadratic closure]] of {{mvar|K}}  which is maximal with respect to being an ordered field with an order extending that of {{mvar|K}}.<ref name=Efr177>Efrat (2006) p. 177</ref> It is also the smallest subfield of the [[algebraic closure]] of {{mvar|K}} that is a Euclidean field and is an ordered [[field extension|extension]] of {{mvar|K}}.
